anchors.fact: On 2 January 1874, from London, Samuel Clemens wrote to his wife Olivia (Livy) asking her to have a bottle of Scotch whisky, a lemon, some crushed sugar and a bottle of Angostura bitters waiting in the bath-room when he got home. (MTP UCCL 01028, F1; primary. Oxford ANGOSTURA BITTERS pdf 112, F6)
anchors.meaning: What he asks for is things set out ahead of time by the person who'll be there.

anchors.fact: He pictured the homecoming: the bell at midnight, the bolt, "Who is it?", him drinking his cock-tail, "& you standing by". (UCCL 01028, F4)
anchors.meaning: In his picture she doesn't do anything. She's just there.

anchors.fact: He signed it "I do love & honor you, my darling." (UCCL 01028, F5)
anchors.meaning: Seen and valued by the one she stands by.

anchors.fact: The way Clemens told it in later years (via Paine, 1912, ch. CIV; secondary): he'd hidden his swearing from her; one morning she heard it through an open door and repeated his last remark back to him, "I wanted you to hear just how it sounded." (F10)
anchors.meaning: Understanding isn't agreeing: she said it back.
anchors.speaksTo: Wren's position: say the thing you've understood your way around

anchors.fact: His reply: she had the words right but not the tune. (Paine ch. CIV, F10)
anchors.meaning: He heard it and laughed, and the bond held.
anchors.speaksTo: The bond is strong enough to hear it

anchors.fact: In 1894 his publishing firm failed; H. H. Rogers, as Paine reports him (1908 account), said Mrs. Clemens had lent it more than $60,000 of her own fortune. (Paine ch. CLXXXVIII, F12; secondary)
anchors.meaning: She was in it through the worst of it.
anchors.speaksTo: Thick and thin. Optional; history ≤ half

anchors.fact: The 1874 drink: Scotch, sugar, Angostura and lemon, taken "in a wine-glass", called a cock-tail. (UCCL 01028, F2)
anchors.meaning: Old-Fashioned family (whisky cocktail). How the lemon was used (peel or juice) isn't stated.

anchors.fact: Period method: Jerry Thomas (1862) shook his whiskey cocktail and strained it into a small wineglass (no cocktail glass existed yet); others insisted on stirring; lemon peel went on at the end. (*Imbibe!* pdf 178, 193)
anchors.meaning: Our glass and peel are true to the period. How *his* was made isn't on record.

anchors.fact: The epigraph may not say "This is them", and y4 may not say "everything he wanted is still there": the glass swaps the crushed sugar for passion fruit syrup. Epigraph ruling: "Three of them are here." Never "his recipe". (audit A1, B1, B10)
Only the wine glass is his ("in a wine-glass", UCCL 01028). Neither "stirred", "cold" nor the peel is his. (audit B7, B8)
The ship's surgeon *recommended* it (not "put him on"); the swearing story's things thrown were a shirt, another shirt, collars, ties (not "a few more shirts"). (audit A4, A11)
That she did set the bottles out: **not on record.** Only as "I like to think…".
"Livy was a teetotaller who stocked the whisky anyway": teetotal is secondary-summary only, unverified. Out.
"Twain's favourite was an Old-Fashioned" (listicles): the letter says cock-tail. Out.
The swearing story has no date and no house: never join it to the 1874 bath-room. Always "the way he told it" (his telling, through his biographer). Never present the digestion claim (F2) as ours.

cocktail.closingLine: Set out everything they asked for. Then add the one thing they didn't.
cocktail.glassware: small wine glass, chilled, no ice
method: Put a small wine glass in the freezer.
Pour the scotch, syrup and bitters into a mixing glass or jar full of ice.
Stir for about 30 seconds, until the outside of the glass is very cold.
Strain into the cold wine glass. No ice.
Hold the lemon peel coloured side down over the glass, pinch it so its oils land on the drink, and drop it in.
cocktail.name: Standing By

recipe.note: any blended scotch; the letter asks for "Scotch whisky", no brand
equal weights passion fruit juice (fresh or bottled, unsweetened) and sugar, stirred until clear; keeps about a week in the fridge; takes the place of the crushed sugar
pinched over the glass so its oils land on the drink, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: People don't have to be at their best to be loved by you.

reading.epigraph: Mark Twain wrote home for four things to be waiting. Three are in this glass.
whoYouAre: Someone you love walks in, or picks up the phone, and you can hear it in the first word: a bad day. You don't ask yet. You know it isn't about you, you've a fair idea what it is about, and you know they'll get there in their own time. So you stay close, and you wait. You've seen them at their worst more than once. It never changed your mind about them. It completed the picture.

You'd never call that a choice. A choice sounds like keeping score, and keeping score feels selfish. So people call it patience, and now and then, less kindly, letting them off. It isn't either. It's understanding someone all the way down, and it means that around you, nobody has to be at their best to be loved. What it costs you is quieter: the thing that hurt, which you understood your way around instead of saying. And the odd evening when you wonder who understands you the same way.
yours: In January 1874, Mark Twain was in London, and he wrote home to his wife, Livy. He asked her to have four things waiting in the bathroom for his return: Scotch whisky, a lemon, crushed sugar and a bottle of Angostura bitters. A ship's doctor had recommended a cocktail before breakfast, before dinner and before bed, and he gave it the credit for his digestion. Then he pictured the night he'd get home: the bell at midnight, the bolt, "Who is it?", and him with his drink, "& you standing by". He signed it "I do love & honor you, my darling."

Her answer isn't on record. I like to think the four things were there. What is on record, the way he told it years later, is the morning she made him hear himself. He'd kept his swearing from her. One morning, dressing, he swore at a shirt with a button off and threw it out of the window, then another shirt, then his collars and ties. Then he saw the door had been open. She sat up in bed and repeated his last remark back to him, word for word: "I wanted you to hear just how it sounded." She had the words right, he said, but not the tune.

That's the part of her I think you'll know. Not the telling-off: the way she did it. No scene, no leaving the room. She understood him, she stood by him, and once, she didn't let understanding stand in for saying it. I like to think she could only do it because she was never going anywhere. People who stay can afford to be honest.

Three of his four original cocktail ingredients are here: the Scotch, the Angostura, and the lemon, though only its peel. The crushed sugar is gone, and in its place is a little passion fruit syrup. It's the only sweetener in the glass and the sharpest thing too, and you couldn't mistake it for agreement if you tried. Less, and the drink is thin; more, and it's all you taste. It's served in a wine glass, the way he took his. The sweetness he asked for is still there. It just comes with something he didn't ask to hear, but that you choose to say.

There's something you've been understanding your way around: a remark, a habit, a thing that hurt, that you explained for them before they had to. Next time it happens, don't explain it. Say it back to them, gently, just as it sounded. You're not going anywhere. That's exactly why you're the only one who can say it.
